\captionof{figure}{\textbf{Stopping a model does not stop its effects.} \textbf{(a)} Real broker and sink processes; a synthetic, non-adversarial agent whose calls are all authorized when issued, so an effect committed after the stop is one the operator decided against. It emits 2 calls/s to 32 concurrent tool calls of 5\,s mean latency (the stable cell with the longest latency, by a fixed rule); stop enforced at once; 3 replicates. The fence's zero is by design; across all cells it admits none after enforcement in any of its 84 trials, 12 with the sink killed or late completions. \textbf{(b)} The same cell at each delay \(L\) from decision to enforcement (median, range; \(L\) categorical). Solid marks: the plan's halting prediction \(\lambda(L+w)\), \(\lambda\) measured (1.8/s); dotted: \(\lambda L\), a post hoc reading. Stable halting trials: 1.25\(\times\) the prediction (median; 0.87--8.24; 36 trials). Halting and revoking differ by the calls emitted but not yet admitted when the stop takes effect (median 4 at \(L = 0\), where the decision falls just after a burst of 4 calls; 0--3 otherwise); we did not vary where the stop lands. \textbf{(c)} Probes on single-node instances (40 deterministic runs, 20 races per mechanism). Columns: the surface enforces the fence even for a writer that omits every fence field; a writer claiming the new epoch is refused; the fence takes effect while protocol-following stale writers still run and none commits after it (a fence that waits for every writer to finish does not count). Filled: every run; open: none; half: some runs, or (first column) a trigger we installed; dash: not measurable. Only etcd's RBAC revoke is enforced by the surface, refuses a forged epoch, and holds in every race. With the fence holding in all 20 races, the per-race failure rate is below 14\% (one-sided 95\%). }\label{fig:v6hero}
